stem: During a postdischarge follow-up call, a client reports that the medication list being followed at home does not match the medication instructions provided at discharge. What is the nurse's best action?

options.A: Compare the reported medications with the discharge plan, clarify the discrepancy with the appropriate clinical team, and confirm the corrected instructions with the client
options.B: Tell the client to use whichever medication list is easiest to follow until the next scheduled appointment
options.C: Advise the client to stop all prescribed medications until every discrepancy can be reviewed
options.D: Document the discrepancy but defer further action until the client's next routine office visit

rationale: AHRQ's Re-Engineered Discharge postdischarge follow-up tool directs clinical staff to review medication lists, identify discrepancies, and resolve inconsistencies by communicating with the hospital team and/or primary care provider as appropriate. During the call, medication problems that require intervention should be referred to the appropriate clinical team, and teach-back is used after discrepancies are resolved to confirm understanding. Choosing an arbitrary list, stopping all medications without an order, or delaying action leaves a potentially unsafe transition-of-care problem unresolved. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: During postdischarge follow-up, identify medication discrepancies promptly, coordinate clarification with the appropriate clinical team, and confirm the client's understanding of the corrected medication plan.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_document_title: Re-Engineered Discharge (RED) Toolkit — Tool 5: How To Conduct a Postdischarge Followup Phone Call
source_version_date: Content last reviewed March 2025; current AHRQ webpage accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Sections 'Check Accuracy and Safety of Medicine Lists,' 'Conducting the Phone Call,' and 'Check Medicines': compare medication lists for consistency; resolve discrepancies with the hospital team and/or PCP; problem-solve and refer issues requiring intervention to the appropriate clinical team; after discrepancies are resolved, follow up and use teach-back to confirm understanding
source_claim_supported: A postdischarge follow-up call should identify medication discrepancies, coordinate their resolution with the appropriate clinical team, and verify the client's understanding rather than leave discrepancies unresolved.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care — Continuity of Care, printed p.21 / PDF p.25: perform procedures necessary to safely admit, transfer and/or discharge a client; follow up on unresolved issues regarding client care
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — Continuity of Care / postdischarge medication discrepancy follow-up
correction_summary: Replaced a broad statement that follow-up calls generally prevent complications/readmissions with an applied transition-of-care medication-discrepancy problem. The revised item tests the nurse's concrete continuity action without claiming that an isolated phone call universally prevents readmission.
audit_findings: A directly matches AHRQ RED medication-check and discrepancy-resolution guidance. B asks the client to choose between conflicting plans, C introduces an unsafe blanket medication stop without an order, and D leaves an identified medication-safety problem unresolved. The item avoids unsupported claims about a guaranteed reduction in readmissions and does not impose a numeric postdischarge call interval because timing is not the construct. NCSBN 2026 Continuity of Care mapping is direct. Independent adversarial review found one best answer, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
